title: Versioning, Compatibility and Error Formats
oneLiner: Which API changes break clients you can't update, how to version when you must, and errors a program can act on.
keyTakeaway: Once an API is public, you can't update its clients, so every change must be backward compatible: adding an optional request field, a new response field or a new endpoint is safe; renaming or removing a field, changing a type, making an optional field required, or tightening validation breaks someone. Clients should be tolerant readers that ignore fields they don't know. When a breaking change is unavoidable, ship it as a new version (/v2 or a dated version header) alongside the old one, announce deprecation with a sunset date, and measure who still calls the old one. Return errors in one consistent, machine-readable shape, such as RFC 9457 Problem Details, with a stable code clients can branch on and a message humans can read.
explanation:
An internal function can be renamed in an afternoon: change it, fix every caller, deploy. A public API can't, because its callers are other people's code: mobile apps that users update months late or never, partner integrations nobody has touched in years, scripts on someone's laptop. The rule that follows is backward compatibility: a new version of the server must keep working for every client written against an older one. A change that would make an existing client fail is a breaking change.

Most of the skill is knowing which changes are which. Safe (additive) changes: a new endpoint, a new optional request parameter with a default that preserves the old behaviour, a new field in a response, a new optional header. Breaking changes: removing or renaming a field or endpoint, changing a field's type (an id from number to string) or format (dollars to cents), making an optional request field required, rejecting input that used to be accepted, changing a default (page size, sort order), changing the meaning of a status code, and changing authentication. Some are breaking only for careless clients: adding a value to an enum breaks a client with a switch statement that throws on unknown values, and adding a response field breaks a client whose JSON deserializer rejects unknown properties. The defence on the client side is the tolerant reader (a pattern Martin Fowler named): read only the fields you need, ignore the rest, and treat unknown enum values as "other". Document that clients must do this, and the safe list gets longer. Behaviour counts too: Hyrum's law says that with enough users, every observable behaviour of an API (the order of results, the exact error text, the timing) will be depended on by somebody.

Protocol Buffers bakes the same rules into the format. Each field has a number, and the binary encoding uses the number, not the name, so renaming a field is safe on the wire but changing its number or type is not. Never reuse the number of a deleted field; mark it reserved. Old readers skip unknown field numbers, which makes adding fields safe in both directions.

When a breaking change is truly needed, version. URL path versioning (/v1/orders, /v2/orders) is the most common: explicit, easy to route and easy to see in logs. Header versioning keeps URLs stable and puts the version in a header or media type (Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json). Stripe uses dated versions: each account is pinned to the API version that was current when it signed up, a request can override it with a Stripe-Version header, and the server runs a chain of small transformations that turn the newest response into each older shape, so the team maintains one codebase rather than one per version. Whatever the scheme, version the whole API rather than each endpoint, make major versions rare, and run old and new side by side. Retiring an old version is a project: announce it, send Deprecation and Sunset headers (the date after which it stops working) on every response, email the owners of the API keys still calling it, and watch the traffic fall before turning it off. For internal APIs between services, the usual approach is expand and contract: add the new field, migrate every consumer, then remove the old field in a later release, so no deploy ever depends on another one happening first.

Errors are part of the contract and need the same care. A good error response uses the right status code (see the REST lesson), has the same shape on every endpoint, and contains a stable, machine-readable code that clients can branch on (card_declined, insufficient_funds), a human-readable message that may change, a pointer to the field that was wrong for validation errors, and a request id that support staff can find in the logs. RFC 9457 Problem Details (which replaced RFC 7807) standardises this as the application/problem+json media type with type (a URI identifying the kind of problem), title, status, detail and instance, plus any extension fields you add. ASP.NET Core and Spring produce it out of the box. Clients should never have to parse the message text to decide what to do; if they do, the text has become part of the API and can never be improved. Don't leak internals in errors either: stack traces, SQL and internal hostnames help attackers, not users.

The widget has three parts: classify ten changes as safe or breaking, watch an old client read a changed response with a strict and a tolerant deserializer, and compare an ad hoc error with a Problem Details error.
